newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia turns away Chinese dissidents.
newsitem.headline: Australia turns away Chinese dissidents.

text.p: Australia will not offer asylum to Chinese dissidents seeking to flee Hong Kong before this year's handover of the British territory to Beijing, a government parliamentarian said on Wednesday.

Peter Nugent, who heads parliament's human rights sub-committee, told Reuters that human rights groups had asked Australia and other nations to give asylum to scores of dissidents and their families who wanted to leave Hong Kong before China regains sovereignty on July 1.
"Human rights groups have been applying pressure, not only on us, but also on a lot of other people, to take more of these people into Australia," Nugent said.
He confirmed local media reports the government was not joining other countries in offering asylum.
"My understanding is that the government has taken the view that we have taken a large number of dissidents...in recent years," he said.
Human rights groups are seeking refuge for up to 80 mainland Chinese dissidents and their families living in Hong Kong.
Human Rights Watch-Asia's Hong Kong director, Robin Monro, told Tuesday's Sydney Morning Herald there had been substantial progress in finding asylum for the Chinese.
Time magazine reported in its latest edition that 40 dissidents hiding in Hong Kong would be granted asylum in the West and secretly flown out of the territory.
The magazine said eight countries, including Britain, the United States and Japan, had offered asylum.
Nugent said Australia had a strong record on helping Chinese dissidents and it was up to other countries, particularly Britain as the current colonial power, to take more.
Australia's former Labor government allowed tens of thousands of Chinese students to remain in Australia after the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre of pro-democracy demonstrators.
A spokesman for Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock told Reuters that the Hong Kong dissidents could apply to come to Australia under the normal immigration processes.
"We have taken a significant number of Chinese nationals who some people might see as dissidents," he said.
Sino-Australian relations have soured since Australia's conservative Liberal-National coalition won power in 1996, foundering on a range of diplomatic and security issues.
